newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela says Malaysia chopper deal being considered.
newsitem.headline: Mandela says Malaysia chopper deal being considered.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Monday the sale of South Africa's Rooivalk combat helicopters to Malaysia was being considered "sympathetically" but no deal had been made yet.
South African radio quoted government sources early on Monday as saying Mandela had sealed an agreement with Malaysia.
But Mandela told reporters on his arrival back in South Africa after a 10-day visit to southeast Asia that talks were ongoing.
"These matters are under discussion. Malaysia is our friend," he said.

"Any proposals of sale of any item that we have will be considered very sympathetically, including weapons, as long as these weapons are going to be used purely for defensive purposes, not for the purpose of destabilising neighbouring countries. I know that Malaysia has no intention of flexing her muscles in regard to other countries."
Mandela said an announcement would be made "in due course" and would not be drawn on details nor a date.
Malaysia's Defence Minister Syed Hamid Albar said earlier on Monday his government was interested in the helicopters, but had yet to decide on the purchase.

The Armaments Corp of South Africa (Armscor), the state's marketing group, has been courting the Malaysian government for more than two years, and renewed its campaign last week with the visit of Mandela to Kuala Lumpur, defence sources said.
But Syed Hamid said the Malaysian government had yet to make a decision on whether to purchase the helicopters.
"We've tested it...It's an attack helicopter and we're interested, but we've not come to a final decision," he told reporters in Kuala Lumpur after talks with French Defence Minister Charles Millon.
The Rooivalk's (Kestrel) manufacturer, Denel, said however that it knew nothing of the deal.
Syed Hamid said U.S., British, Russian and French helicopter manufacturers were also offering machines to Malaysia and his government would base its decision on price and technology.

"The helicopter may be the best in the world but it still has to suit our needs," Syed Hamid said. "Suffice to say, the Rooivalk has the capability to fulfill at least part of our air force requirement."
He said if the purchase went through, the deal would include a local components manufacturing facility for the Rooivalk.

Malaysia has been building up its military capability in recent years, buying F-18 jets from the United States, MiG-29 fighters from Russia and armoured personnel carriers from South Korea while denying it was involved in an arms race.
The government's biggest defence project is a 15-year programme to acquire 27 naval patrol boats at a cost of 5.0 billion ringgit ($2 billion).
